issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items 'others can see what happened to me' and 'ashamed of what happened to my body' imply a trauma with visible bodily violation or injury, most classically interpersonal/sexual trauma, and are hard to reconcile with a generic man-made disaster trauma in the absence of any corroborating memory or trigger content about bodily injury or disfigurement.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Being Touched' is specifically linked to bodily violation/contact-based trauma and fits poorly with the rest of the profile for man-made disaster. The threat items center on environmental danger and escape planning, creating a cross-node mismatch with this touch-avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma with prominent bodily violation or physical injury consequences. For a man-made disaster trauma, this specific body-focused pattern is not impossible, but in the absence of any supporting memory or trigger content and alongside the other items emphasizing generalized danger, it stands out as a hard-to-explain shift toward an assault/injury formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Within the current profile, avoidance of touch and bodily stress appears organized around bodily harm/shame, but the threat items are about environmental danger, escape planning, and unfamiliar places. That makes the strategy set only partially connected to the expressed threat/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise centered on persistent danger, vigilance, scanning, escape planning, and avoidance of unfamiliar places, which coheres with threat-focused beliefs after a man-made disaster. 'Failed Role' introduces a distinct self-evaluative theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and is hard to reconcile with this otherwise purely danger/safety formulation. Given the active formulation emphasizes Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a danger-based appraisal would better fit the linked hypervigilance and checking strategies than a role-failure appraisal.

vignette:
Meera was thirty-two years old, a single woman who had built her life around service and scrutiny. As a city council member in a mid-sized American city, she was used to navigating crowded town halls, tense negotiations, and the unpredictable energy of public meetings. That world ended on an evening two years ago, when a propane tank exploded at a community festival she had helped organize. She was standing near the stage when the blast tore through a food vendor’s tent, sending a fireball rolling across the park. In the chaos that followed—screaming, the smell of burnt metal, people running in every direction—Meera found herself pinned beneath a collapsed table, her leg trapped, unable to move as flames licked at the grass a few yards away. A stranger pulled her out, but in those minutes, she had been certain she was going to die.

In the months after, Meera could not shake the feeling that the world had become a place where disaster was always waiting. She began to believe that safety was an illusion, that she had to be on guard all the time, that you never knew what could happen next. This conviction grew into a constant, exhausting vigilance. She came to see the world as fundamentally dangerous, and that belief shaped everything she did. Because she was certain that danger could strike at any moment, she started scanning her environment constantly—checking for anything unusual, any person who seemed too close or too still. She became especially careful around people she did not know. At council meetings, she would study the audience before speaking, noting exits, watching hands and faces. She found herself planning escape routes everywhere she went: before sitting down in a restaurant, before entering a colleague’s office, before stepping into an elevator. She could not feel comfortable in unfamiliar places at all, so she avoided them entirely, sticking to a narrow circuit of home, city hall, and one grocery store she knew by heart.

Nighttime was worse. Meera found it harder to feel safe after dark, and she began to dread evening events. She would leave community meetings early, claiming fatigue. She stopped attending the late-night hearings that had once been part of her routine. The vigilance she maintained during the day became unbearable at night, when shadows and silence amplified her sense of threat. And because she was always scanning, always planning, always avoiding, her sense of danger never receded. Each time she checked her surroundings and found nothing, she felt only a temporary relief, followed by the renewed certainty that the next moment would be different. Her hypervigilance toward people—watching for anyone who seemed aggressive, erratic, or simply out of place—kept her in a state of low-grade alarm that fed back into her belief that the world was unsafe. She was constantly on edge, and that edge only sharpened her conviction that she had to be more careful.

The consequences were concrete. Her colleagues noticed she was distracted, less available. She stopped attending neighborhood walks and street festivals, events that had been central to her work. Her chief of staff gently suggested she seemed burned out. Meera knew it was more than that. She had begun to feel trapped in her own life, unable to trust the spaces and people she had once navigated with ease. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment of public failure: at a council vote on emergency preparedness funding, she froze when a constituent raised a question about gas line safety. Her mind went blank. She could not speak. She excused herself and did not return.

Now, sitting in a therapist’s office, Meera was terrified that she would never feel safe again. But she was also exhausted—too tired to keep scanning, too tired to keep planning escape routes, too tired to believe that her vigilance was keeping her alive. She hoped, more than anything, that someone could show her how to stop.
